network-delay-time.pattern: Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights (Dijkstra)

approaches.name: Bellman–Ford: relax every edge n − 1 times
approaches.idea: A shortest path uses at most n − 1 edges. Starting with `dist[k] = 0`, relaxing every edge n − 1 times makes every distance final. The answer is the largest distance, or −1 if some node stays unreachable.
steps: Set `dist[k] = 0` and every other distance to ∞.
Repeat n − 1 times: for every edge `u → v` of weight `w`, if `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]`.
If any distance is still ∞, return −1; otherwise return the maximum distance.
approaches.why: n − 1 rounds over all E edges. Slower than Dijkstra, but it also handles negative edge weights.

approaches.name: Dijkstra with a min-heap
approaches.idea: Always settle the unsettled node with the smallest known distance; with non-negative weights, no later path can make it shorter. Relax its outgoing edges and continue.
steps: Build adjacency lists. Push `(0, k)` into a min-heap; `dist[k] = 0`.
Pop `(d, u)`; skip it if `d > dist[u]` (an outdated entry).
For each edge `u → v` with weight `w`, if `d + w < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]` and push `(dist[v], v)`.
Return the largest distance, or −1 if some node was never reached.
approaches.why: Each edge can push one heap entry, and each heap operation costs O(log E) = O(log V).

path-with-minimum-effort.pattern: Minimax path: Dijkstra where a path's cost is its largest step (or binary search + BFS)

approaches.name: Binary search the effort, check with BFS
approaches.idea: For a limit `E`, ask: can you reach the corner using only steps with height difference ≤ `E`? That is a plain BFS, and if it works for `E` it works for anything larger. Binary search the smallest `E`.
steps: Search `E` in `[0, 10⁶]`.
BFS from the top-left using only moves whose height difference is at most `E`; see whether the bottom-right is reached.
If reachable, `hi = E`; else `lo = E + 1`. Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About 20 BFS runs (H = 10⁶ is the height range), each O(m·n).

approaches.name: Dijkstra on the largest step so far
approaches.idea: Let `effort[cell]` be the smallest possible "largest step" of a path to it. Extending a path with a step of size `d` gives effort `max(current, d)`, which never decreases — so Dijkstra still works with `max` in place of `+`.
steps: Set `effort[0][0] = 0` and push it into a min-heap.
Pop the cell with the smallest effort; if it is the bottom-right, return it (skip outdated entries).
For each neighbour, `candidate = max(effort, |height difference|)`; if smaller than its recorded effort, record and push it.
approaches.why: Each cell has 4 edges, so O(m·n) heap pushes of O(log(m·n)) each.

cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.pattern: Bellman–Ford limited to k + 1 rounds (shortest path with at most k + 1 edges)

approaches.name: DFS over every route with at most k + 1 flights
approaches.idea: Explore every route from `src` that uses at most k + 1 flights, and keep the cheapest one that ends at `dst`. Prune routes that already cost more than the best found.
steps: `dfs(city, flightsLeft, cost)`: if `cost >= best`, stop; if `city == dst`, record `cost`.
If flights remain, follow every outgoing flight with `flightsLeft − 1`.
Start with `dfs(src, k + 1, 0)` and return the best, or −1.
approaches.why: With out-degree d, the number of routes grows exponentially in k; pruning helps but does not change the worst case.

approaches.name: Bellman–Ford for exactly k + 1 rounds
approaches.idea: After round `i` of Bellman–Ford, `dist` holds the cheapest prices using at most `i` flights — as long as each round reads the previous round's values (a copy), so one round cannot chain several flights together.
steps: Set `dist[src] = 0`, all others ∞.
Repeat k + 1 times: copy `dist` to `next`; for each flight `u → v` with price `p`, if `dist[u] + p < next[v]`, set `next[v]`. Then `dist = next`.
Return `dist[dst]`, or −1 if it is still ∞.
approaches.why: k + 1 rounds over all E flights, with two arrays of size V. Plain Dijkstra fails here, because the cheapest path might use too many stops.

path-with-maximum-probability.pattern: Dijkstra for a "best product" path (max-heap; probabilities only shrink along a path)

approaches.name: Bellman–Ford style relaxation until nothing improves
approaches.idea: Keep the best known probability for each node. Repeatedly go over every edge (both directions) and improve a node if reaching it through the edge gives a higher product. Stop when a full pass changes nothing.
steps: Set `prob[start] = 1`, others 0.
Repeat up to n − 1 times: for each edge `(a, b, p)`, update `prob[b]` with `prob[a]·p` and `prob[a]` with `prob[b]·p` if larger.
Stop early when a pass makes no change; return `prob[end]`.
approaches.why: At most n − 1 passes over E edges; the early stop makes it fast on most inputs.

approaches.name: Dijkstra with a max-heap
approaches.idea: Multiplying by a probability ≤ 1 can only keep a value the same or make it smaller — the mirror image of adding a non-negative weight. So Dijkstra works with a max-heap: the node with the highest probability popped first is final.
steps: Build adjacency lists with probabilities (both directions).
Push `(1, start)`; `best[start] = 1`.
Pop the largest probability; if it is the end node, return it; skip outdated entries.
For each neighbour, if `p·edge > best[nb]`, update and push. Return 0 if the end is never reached.
approaches.why: Each edge can cause one push, at O(log V) per heap operation.

minimum-obstacle-removal-to-reach-corner.pattern: 0-1 BFS: edges cost 0 or 1, so a deque replaces Dijkstra's heap

approaches.name: Dijkstra: entering an obstacle costs 1
approaches.idea: Treat each cell as a node; moving into a cell costs its value (1 for an obstacle, 0 for empty). The answer is the cheapest path cost from the top-left to the bottom-right.
steps: Set `cost[0][0] = 0`; push it into a min-heap.
Pop the cheapest cell (skip outdated entries); if it is the target, return its cost.
For each neighbour, `cand = cost + grid[neighbour]`; if better, record and push.
approaches.why: Standard Dijkstra over m·n cells with 4 edges each. Correct, but the heap is more than needed when costs are only 0 or 1.

approaches.name: 0-1 BFS with a deque
approaches.idea: When every edge costs 0 or 1, a deque keeps the frontier sorted for free: push a 0-cost neighbour to the front and a 1-cost neighbour to the back. Cells then leave the deque in order of cost, just as in Dijkstra.
steps: Set `cost[0][0] = 0` and put it in a deque.
Pop from the front. For each neighbour, `cand = cost + grid[neighbour]`; if it improves the neighbour, record it.
Push the neighbour to the front if the step cost 0, otherwise to the back.
Return `cost` of the bottom-right cell.
approaches.why: Each cell is improved at most twice (its cost can only be one of two adjacent values while it waits), and deque operations are O(1).

minimum-cost-to-make-at-least-one-valid-.pattern: 0-1 BFS: following a sign costs 0, going any other way costs 1

approaches.name: Dijkstra over cells
approaches.idea: From each cell you may move in all four directions: moving where the sign points is free, any other direction costs 1 (changing the sign). The answer is the cheapest path cost.
steps: Directions 1..4 = right, left, down, up.
Dijkstra from the top-left: pop the cheapest cell, skip outdated entries, stop at the bottom-right.
For each direction `k`, the step costs 0 if `k == grid[r][c]`, else 1; relax the neighbour.
approaches.why: Each cell has 4 edges, giving O(m·n) heap operations of O(log(m·n)).

approaches.name: 0-1 BFS with a deque
approaches.idea: Edge costs are only 0 (follow the sign) or 1 (change it), so a deque gives the Dijkstra order without a heap: 0-cost moves go to the front, 1-cost moves to the back.
steps: Set `cost[0][0] = 0` and push it.
Pop from the front; for each direction compute the step cost (0 if it matches the sign) and relax the neighbour.
On an improvement, push to the front for cost 0 and to the back for cost 1.
Return the bottom-right cost.
approaches.why: Constant work per cell and edge, since deque operations are O(1).

swim-in-rising-water.pattern: Minimax path: Dijkstra on the highest cell so far (or binary search + BFS)

approaches.name: Binary search the time, check with BFS
approaches.idea: At time `t` you may use every cell with height ≤ `t`. Being able to cross at time `t` means you can at any later time, so binary search the smallest `t` for which a BFS through cells ≤ `t` connects the corners.
steps: Search `t` in `[grid[0][0], n² − 1]`.
BFS from `(0, 0)` through cells with height ≤ `t`; check whether `(n − 1, n − 1)` is reached.
If yes, `hi = t`; else `lo = t + 1`. Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About log₂(n²) BFS runs of O(n²) each.

approaches.name: Dijkstra on the highest cell on the path
approaches.idea: The time a route needs is the highest cell on it. Expand cells in order of that value with a min-heap: the first time the bottom-right cell is popped, its value is the answer.
steps: Push `(grid[0][0], 0, 0)`; mark `(0, 0)` visited.
Pop the cell with the lowest "highest so far" `t`; if it is the bottom-right, return `t`.
For each unvisited neighbour, mark it and push `(max(t, height), r, c)`.
approaches.why: Each of the n² cells is pushed once, with O(log n²) = O(log n) per heap operation.

find-the-city-with-the-smallest-number-o.pattern: All-pairs shortest paths (Floyd–Warshall, or Dijkstra from every city)

approaches.name: Floyd–Warshall
approaches.idea: Compute the shortest distance between every pair of cities: for each possible middle city `k`, a route `i → k → j` may beat the best known `i → j`. Then count, for each city, the others within the threshold.
steps: Initialise `dist[i][i] = 0`, `dist[u][v] = dist[v][u] = w` for each road, others ∞.
For `k`, then `i`, then `j`: `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])`.
For each city, count `j != i` with `dist[i][j] <= threshold`; keep the smallest count, preferring the larger city number on ties (scan with `<=`).
approaches.why: n³ = 10⁶ relaxations for n = 100, and an n × n table. Simple and ideal for a small, dense graph.

approaches.name: Dijkstra from every city
approaches.idea: Run Dijkstra from each city; it can stop expanding once distances exceed the threshold. Count the cities reached within it.
steps: Build adjacency lists (roads go both ways).
For each city `s`, run Dijkstra, not pushing anything farther than the threshold; count settled cities other than `s`.
Return the city with the smallest count, choosing the larger number on ties.
approaches.why: n Dijkstra runs of O(E log n). For sparse graphs this beats O(n³); for this dense limit both are fast.
